intro: Competitive cycling ranges from one-day classics and three-week Grand Tours on the road to explosive sprints on a banked indoor track. Riders race as teams, sheltering in each other's slipstream to save energy, and tactics matter as much as legs. The Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) publishes the regulations for every discipline.
inThirtySeconds: On the road, first across the line wins the stage — but stage races are won on total time.
Riding in another rider's slipstream (drafting) saves a lot of energy and is legal in road races.
Riders finishing together in a bunch get the same time.
Time trials are raced alone against the clock — no drafting.
objective: Cross the finish line first in a one-day race, or have the lowest cumulative time across all stages of a stage race.

facts.players: Individuals within teams (road teams of up to eight in Grand Tours)
facts.duration: From under a minute (track sprints) to 3 weeks (Grand Tours)
facts.environment: Roads, velodromes, mountain-bike trails and BMX tracks

scoring.label: General classification
scoring.detail: The sum of each rider's stage times, minus any time bonuses.

scoring.label: Points classification
scoring.detail: Awarded for placings at finishes and intermediate sprints.

scoring.label: Mountains classification
scoring.detail: Awarded for reaching the top of categorised climbs first.

variants.name: Road
variants.description: One-day races and multi-day stage races on public roads.

variants.name: Track
variants.description: Races on a banked oval velodrome with fixed-gear bikes and no brakes.

chapters.title: Stage races
chapters.summary: How a Grand Tour is won.

rules.title: General classification
rules.summary: The overall winner is the rider with the lowest total time after all stages.
rules.body: This is why a rider can win a Grand Tour without winning a stage: consistent finishes and strong time trials add up. Leaders of classifications wear distinctive jerseys, such as the yellow jersey at the Tour de France.
rules.example: A rider finishes every mountain stage within seconds of the winners and gains a minute in the time trial: they can take the overall title without a single stage win.

rules.title: Same time for the bunch
rules.summary: Riders who finish together in a group are given the same time as the first rider in that group.
rules.body: Gaps appear only when there is a visible split in the group. To protect overall contenders from crashes in chaotic sprints, riders delayed by an incident close to the finish of flat stages are credited with the time of their group.

rules.title: Time cut
rules.summary: Riders who finish too far behind the stage winner can be eliminated.
rules.body: The cut-off is a percentage of the winner's time, depending on the stage's difficulty and speed. Jury decisions occasionally relax it if a large group misses it.

rules.title: Drafting and team tactics
rules.summary: In road races, riders may shelter behind others to save energy; teammates work to protect their leader.
rules.body: Domestiques fetch bottles, chase breakaways and lead out sprinters. Pushing or pulling other riders, or holding onto team cars, is forbidden.

rules.title: Time trials
rules.summary: Riders start at intervals and race alone against the clock; drafting behind other riders is not allowed.
rules.body: Specialised aerodynamic bikes and positions are permitted within UCI technical limits. Team time trials see a team ride together, timed on a specified finisher.

rules.title: Track sprint
rules.summary: Two or three riders race over three laps; only the final 200 m is timed, so the early laps are a tactical game of cat and mouse.
rules.body: Riders must not cross into an opponent's path in the final straight, and the sprinter's lane on the inside of the track has strict rules about overtaking.

rules.title: Keirin
rules.summary: Riders follow a motorised pacer that gradually speeds up and pulls off with laps to go, leaving a flat-out sprint.
rules.body: Overtaking the pacer before it leaves the track leads to relegation or disqualification. The event originated in Japan.

fouls.name: Irregular sprinting
fouls.description: Deviating from your line to block or endanger others.

fouls.name: Holding onto a vehicle
fouls.description: Getting a tow from a team car or motorbike.

fouls.name: Littering outside zones
fouls.description: Discarding bottles or wrappers outside designated areas.

fouls.name: Technical fraud
fouls.description: Illegal equipment such as hidden motors.

flow.title: Neutral start
flow.description: The peloton rolls out behind the race director before the flag drops.

flow.title: Breakaway
flow.description: A small group escapes; the peloton controls the gap.

flow.title: Climbs and sprints
flow.description: Intermediate points and mountain summits shape the jerseys.

flow.title: Finale
flow.description: Lead-out trains or attacks on the final climb decide the stage.

positions.name: Team leader
positions.role: The rider aiming for the overall or race win.

positions.name: Domestique
positions.role: Support rider who works for the leader.

positions.name: Climber
positions.role: Light rider who excels in the mountains.

positions.name: Rouleur
positions.role: Powerful rider for flat terrain and time trials.

field.name: Road course / velodrome
field.dimensions: Road stages often 150–250 km; Olympic velodromes are typically 250 m laps
field.surface: Tarmac (and sometimes cobbles or gravel); wooden track in velodromes
notes: Feed zones and finish-line timing on the road

funFacts: The first Tour de France, in 1903, had only six stages — some longer than 400 km.
A rider in a large peloton can save a significant share of their energy compared with riding alone.
